theory.overview: Exception handling provides structured error recovery without propagating error codes through every function. When an exception is thrown, the runtime unwinds the stack, looking for an appropriate catch handler. Understanding exceptions helps write robust code and debug stack traces.

sections.title: Throw and Catch
sections.content: Throwing creates an exception object and begins stack unwinding. Catch blocks specify which exception types they handle. Uncaught exceptions terminate the program.

sections.title: Stack Unwinding
sections.content: As the stack unwinds, destructors run for local objects (in C++), finally blocks execute (in Java/Python), and frame-by-frame cleanup occurs until a handler is found.

sections.title: Zero-Cost Exceptions
sections.content: Modern implementations use exception tables to avoid overhead when no exceptions occur. The cost is only paid when an exception is actually thrown.

keyConcepts.name: Exception Object
keyConcepts.description: Contains error information and stack trace

keyConcepts.name: Landing Pad
keyConcepts.description: Code location where exception handler begins

steps.title: Throwing an Exception
steps.content: The throw statement creates an exception object and initiates stack unwinding. Control transfers to the first matching catch block up the call stack.

steps.title: Unwinding Process
steps.content: For each stack frame: 1) Locate exception table entry for current PC, 2) Run destructors for local objects, 3) Check for catch handler, 4) Pop frame if no handler found.

steps.title: Matching Handlers
steps.content: The runtime checks exception type against catch parameters. Inheritance hierarchies are respected (catch Derived matches Base* handlers). Ellipsis (...) catches everything.

practiceProblems.title: Stack Unwinding
practiceProblems.description: Function A calls B, B calls C, C throws. B has catch, A has catch. Where is the exception caught?
practiceProblems.solution: Caught in B. Unwinding stops at the first matching handler, so B's catch receives control.

practiceProblems.title: RAII & Exceptions
practiceProblems.description: Why does RAII work well with exceptions?
practiceProblems.solution: Destructors are called during stack unwinding, guaranteeing cleanup of resources (memory, locks, files) even when exceptions occur.
